title: I like it, I don't like it
goal: Say what you like and dislike at different strengths, and choose the right article after verbs of liking.
bekal: building a ladder of taste from *adorer* to *détester*
using **le, la, les** after verbs of liking — always
joining two verbs with no change of form
wave: Review **Unit 13** first: order a full three-course dinner from memory, then give your opinion on each dish.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Les goûts et les couleurs
dialogs.intro: Camille and Budi talk about their tastes while waiting for the bus.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: J'aime bien, mais je préfère les films d'action.
lines.id: I do, but I prefer action movies.
lines.literal: I-like well, but I prefer the films of-action.

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: Moi, j'adore les vieux films. Surtout en noir et blanc.
lines.id: Me, I love old movies. Especially black-and-white ones.
lines.literal: me, I-adore the films old. above-all in black and white.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Vraiment ? Moi, je trouve ça un peu lent.
lines.id: Really? I find them a bit slow.
lines.literal: really? me, I find that a-little slow.

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: Et la musique ? Tu écoutes quoi ?
lines.id: And music? What do you listen to?
lines.literal: and the music? you listen what?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: J'aime beaucoup le jazz. Je déteste le rap.
lines.id: I really like jazz. I hate rap.
lines.literal: I-like much the jazz. I hate the rap.

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: Tu détestes tout le rap ? C'est sévère !
lines.id: You hate all rap? That's harsh!
lines.literal: you hate all the rap? it-is hard!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bon, disons que je n'aime pas trop. Et toi ?
lines.id: Well, let's say I'm not a big fan. What about you?
lines.literal: well, let's-say that I not-like not too-much. and you?

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: J'aime tout, sauf le métal. Ça me fatigue.
lines.id: I like everything except metal. It wears me out.
lines.literal: I-like everything, except the metal. that me tires.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tu aimes cuisiner ? On pourrait faire un dîner.
lines.id: Do you like cooking? We could make dinner.
lines.literal: you like to-cook? one could make a dinner.

lines.speaker: Camille:
lines.text: J'adore cuisiner ! Mais je déteste faire la vaisselle.
lines.id: I love cooking! But I hate doing the dishes.
lines.literal: I-adore to-cook! but I hate to-make the dishes.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Alors c'est parfait. Tu cuisines, je lave.
lines.id: Then it's perfect. You cook, I'll wash up.
lines.literal: then it-is perfect. you cook, I wash.

notes: **After verbs of liking, always le, la, les.** *J'aime **le** café*, not *j'aime du café*. It makes sense once you think about it: what you like is coffee as a whole, not some amount of coffee. Compare *je bois **du** café* (I drink some coffee).

**And the article survives in negative sentences.** *Je n'aime pas **le** café* — here *le* doesn't shrink to *de*, unlike *je ne bois pas **de** café*. This is the one big exception to the rule you set up in Unit 4.

**Aimer has two faces.** For things and activities, it means "like". For people, *je t'aime* means "I love you" — so be careful. To say you like someone without a misunderstanding, add *bien*: *je t'aime **bien*** = I like you (as a friend).
**Adorer isn't over the top.** In everyday French, *j'adore* simply means "I love", not "I worship". People use it for coffee, movies, and socks without sounding strange at all.

**Two verbs in a row: the second stays in the infinitive.** *J'aime **cuisiner***, *je déteste **faire** la vaisselle*, *je préfère **regarder** un film*. The infinitive never changes, whoever the subject is.
**Ça me fatigue** — literally "that tires me". A very common pattern for feelings: *ça m'énerve* (that annoys me), *ça me plaît* (I like that), *ça m'intéresse* (that interests me).
**Sauf** = except. A little word that saves many conversations: *j'aime tout, sauf…*

grammars.title: The ladder of taste
body: From liking most to liking least. All are followed by *le, la, les* or an infinitive.
after: ⚠️ *J'aime bien* is actually **weaker** than *j'aime* — not what English speakers expect from a word meaning "well". Adding *bien* softens, it doesn't strengthen. What strengthens is *beaucoup*.
*Préférer* changes é to è in four forms: *je préfère, tu préfères, il préfère, ils préfèrent*, but *nous préférons, vous préférez*. The same pattern as *se lever* in Unit 8.

grammars.title: Hobbies and free time
body: Verbs for leisure activities. Watch the prepositions — each one has its own preference.
after: *Jouer à* for games, *jouer de* for instruments. A one-letter difference that completely changes the meaning: *je joue du piano* (I play the piano) versus *je joue au piano* — which means nothing.
The usual merging applies: *jouer à + le = au*, *jouer de + le = du*.

blocks.title: Asking about tastes
items: *Qu'est-ce que tu aimes faire ?* — What do you like doing?
*Tu aimes le sport ?* — Do you like sports?
*Qu'est-ce que tu préfères, le thé ou le café ?* — Which do you prefer, tea or coffee?
*Ça te plaît ?* — Do you like it?
*Moi aussi.* / *Moi non plus.* — Me too. / Me neither.
⚠️ Agreeing with a negative sentence takes *moi non plus*, not *moi aussi* — just like "me neither". "I don't like coffee." — "*Moi non plus.*"
